languages.name: Finnish
languages.where: Finland; minorities in Sweden, Norway, Russia, Estonia
languages.note: Agglutinative with rich case system and consonant gradation; conservative among Finnic languages. Contains many early loanwords from Baltic (e.g. tytär 'daughter'), Germanic (kuningas 'king') and later Swedish and Russian.

languages.name: Meänkieli
languages.where: Tornedalen (Torne Valley), northern Sweden
languages.note: Finnish dialect continuum of the Torne Valley, recognised as a separate minority language in Sweden in 2000. Diverged from Finland Finnish through a border drawn in 1809 and heavy Swedish lexical influence. Low-confidence word forms (no published source found): two (kaksi), three (kolme), mother (äiti), night (yö), sun (aurinko), name (nimi), heart (sydän), new (uusi), fish (kala), winter (talvi).

languages.name: Kven
languages.where: Northern Norway (Troms and Finnmark)
languages.note: Descended from Finnish dialects brought by 18th-19th century migrants to northern Norway; recognised as a minority language in 2005. Strong Norwegian loan influence and heavy assimilation pressure. Low-confidence word forms (no published source found): two (kaksi), three (kolme), mother (äiti), night (yö), sun (aurinko), name (nimi), heart (sydän), new (uusi), fish (kala), winter (talvi).

languages.name: Karelian
languages.where: Republic of Karelia (Russia), Tver region; small group in Finland
languages.note: Closely related to Finnish but with its own phonology and vocabulary; spoken by a shrinking population in Russia. Much Russian lexical and grammatical influence, and used also in Tver Karelian dialects displaced there in the 17th century.

sources.water: NorthEuraLex 0.9 (Dellert et al. 2020); Wiktionary translations of 'water'
sources.name: NorthEuraLex 0.9 (Dellert et al. 2020)

languages.name: Livvi (Olonets Karelian)
languages.where: Southern Karelia around Olonets (Aunus), Russia
languages.note: Dialect group of Karelian between Karelian proper and Veps, with a literary standard since the 1990s. Many Russian loanwords; influenced earlier by Ladoga-area Veps.

languages.name: Ludic
languages.where: Northwest of Lake Onega, Republic of Karelia, Russia
languages.note: Transitional Finnic idiom between Karelian and Veps, spoken by very few elderly people. Strong Russian influence; some scholars classify it as a Karelian dialect. Low-confidence word forms (no published source found): one (yks'), two (kaks').

languages.name: Veps
languages.where: South of Lake Onega and Lake Ladoga, Russia
languages.note: Archaic Finnic language with no consonant gradation and a vowel system unlike Karelian. Pressed by Russian; Veps people were historically part of the Beloozero region of early Rus.

sources.night: NorthEuraLex 0.9 (Dellert et al. 2020); Wiktionary translations of 'night'
sources.name: NorthEuraLex 0.9 (Dellert et al. 2020)

languages.name: Ingrian
languages.where: Ingria (Leningrad Oblast), Russia
languages.note: Finnic language of the Izhorians, spoken now by a handful of elderly speakers. Long contact with Votic, Russian and Finnish settlers (Ingrian Finns) who largely replaced it.

languages.name: Votic
languages.where: Ingria, Leningrad Oblast, Russia
languages.note: Closest to Estonian in several features but with unique archaic traits; the last native speakers number under ten. Long Russian pressure and WWII displacement ended transmission.

languages.name: Estonian
languages.where: Estonia; diaspora in Finland, Sweden, Russia, USA
languages.note: Official language of Estonia, lost vowel harmony and nearly lost final vowels; three phonemic length degrees. Heavily shaped by Low German, Swedish, Baltic Germans, and Russian contact over centuries.

languages.name: Võro (South Estonian)
languages.where: Southeastern Estonia (Võrumaa, Setomaa) and Pskov region
languages.note: The most distinct form of Estonian, descending from the first branch to split from Proto-Finnic; has a glottal-stop phoneme and retained vowel harmony traces. Contact with Latvian and Russian neighbours; Seto variety is Orthodox. Low-confidence word forms (no published source found): mother (imä), winter (tal'v).

languages.name: Livonian
languages.where: Courland coast (Kurzeme), Latvia
languages.note: The last native speaker died in 2013; a small revival community with some second-language speakers remains. Stød-like tone distinction and strong Latvian and Low German influence; once spoken across Livonia up to the Daugava.

sources.two: NorthEuraLex 0.9 (Dellert et al. 2020); Wiktionary translations of 'two'

languages.name: Northern Sami
languages.where: Northern Norway, Sweden and Finland
languages.note: The largest Sami language, with 70-90 percent of all Sami speakers; recognised in Norway, Sweden and Finland. Consonant gradation and a vigesimal-free number system; notable early Germanic (Norse) and later Scandinavian and Finnish loans.

languages.where: Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Yamal, northern Russia
languages.note: The most widespread Samoyedic language, spoken by reindeer herders over a vast tundra area. Russian influence is increasing; Komi and Khanty contacts older. Low-confidence word forms (no published source found): one (ŋopoi).

nodes.name: Proto-Uralic
nodes.note: Reconstructed ancestor of all Uralic languages; the homeland is placed variously in the Volga-Kama area or west of the Urals. Estimates range widely; the cautious modern view (Häkkinen, Aikio, Kallio) treats the family as a comb/rake of early diverging branches rather than a clean Finno-Ugric versus Samoyedic split.
sources: Honkola et al. 2013, J. Evol. Biol. 26(6)

nodes.name: Proto-Samoyedic
nodes.note: Branch spoken in Siberia; connection to the rest of Uralic is through the poorly attested early separation. Dating relies on glottochronology and typology, so very uncertain.
sources: Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (Proto-Samoyedic c. 2000-2500 years ago)

nodes.name: Proto-Ugric
nodes.note: Ancestor of Hungarian and the Ob-Ugric languages (Khanty, Mansi). The Ugric unity itself is questioned by some scholars; the split put Hungarians on a migration path ending in the Carpathian Basin by c. 895 CE.
sources: Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (branch-internal ages, general bound)

nodes.name: Proto-Permic
nodes.note: Common ancestor of Komi and Udmurt, with shared Iranian and early Turkic loans. The Finno-Permic grouping linking Permic to Finnic and Mari is now treated cautiously.
sources: Honkola et al. 2013, J. Evol. Biol. 26(6) (as summarised in Honkola's thesis; full text not accessible)

nodes.name: Proto-Mari
nodes.note: Common ancestor of Meadow and Hill Mari; only Meadow Mari is shown here. Placed on its own branch, since the Finno-Volgaic grouping with Mordvinic is doubted.
sources: Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (branch-internal ages, general bound)

nodes.name: Proto-Mordvinic
nodes.note: Split into Erzya and Moksha, tied to the settlement of the Volga and Oka basins; evidence from loanwords (Iranian, Turkic, Slavic) and dialect geography. Grouping with Finnic (Finno-Volgaic) is disputed, so Mordvinic is shown separately.
sources: Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (branch-internal ages, general bound)

nodes.name: Proto-Sami
nodes.note: Spread across Fennoscandia in the first millennium CE after language shift from older, unknown Palaeo-Laplandic languages (Aikio); dated by Proto-Germanic and Proto-Finnic loans and by internal divergence. Relation to Finnic through shared Uralic roots is not a closer sisterhood than the others.
sources: Aikio 2012 / Kallio-Aikio chronology (via academia.edu abstract: disintegration of Late Proto-Saami c. 200 CE)
Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (Saamic spread; northern/eastern Saamic across N Fennoscandia by 500-700 CE)
Honkola et al. 2013, J. Evol. Biol. 26(6) (as summarised in Honkola's thesis; full text not accessible)

nodes.name: West Sami
nodes.note: Group including South, Ume, Pite, Lule and North Sami, in Fennoscandia west of the Gulf of Bothnia. The East/West division is a dialect-continuum split rather than a clean tree. No published date was found for this specific split; the date is a low-confidence estimate.

nodes.name: East Sami
nodes.note: Inari, Skolt, Kildin and Ter Sami; East Sami speakers occupy Finland and the Kola peninsula. No published date was found for this specific split; the date is a low-confidence estimate.

nodes.name: Proto-Finnic
nodes.note: Reconstructed around the Gulf of Finland; dated from Baltic and Germanic loanwords showing a unified Proto-Finnic after contact with Proto-Baltic and before 500 CE (Kallio). Treated here as a direct branch of Uralic, not as a daughter of Finno-Permic or Finno-Volgaic.

nodes.name: South Estonian
nodes.note: South Estonian (Võro, Seto) branched off first from the rest of Finnic, preserving archaic features; supported by dialect geography and phonological innovations that other Finnic languages share. No published date was found for this specific split; the date is a low-confidence estimate.

nodes.name: North Finnic
nodes.note: Remaining Finnic varieties after South Estonian split. Internal groupings (Coastal, Karelian, Finnish) are partly a dialect continuum; some scholars prefer a network model. No published date was found for this specific split; the date is a low-confidence estimate.

nodes.name: Coastal Finnic
nodes.note: Estonian, Votic and Livonian group on the southern Gulf of Finland and Baltic coast; labels such as Southern Finnic are used differently by different scholars. No published date was found for this specific split; the date is a low-confidence estimate.

nodes.name: Karelian-Veps cluster
nodes.note: Eastern Finnic varieties around Ladoga and Onega, including Karelian, Livvi, Ludic, Veps and Ingrian. Ingrian is sometimes linked with Finnish; the grouping reflects geography.
sources: Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (Karelian to southern Karelia early centuries CE, northward spread c. 900 CE)
Novgorod birchbark letter 292 (c. 13th c., earliest Karelian text)

nodes.name: Finnish dialect cluster
nodes.note: Finnish dialects from which Meänkieli and Kven later emerged through 18th-19th century migration and border changes.
sources: Grünthal et al. 2022, Diachronica 39(4) (ancestral Finnish in SE Finland early centuries CE; northward spread c. 900 CE)
